Task 6: Path to Market Task Summary: This task will provide the necessary technical information that can help develop the commercialization strategy. The following attributes will be developed based on engineering modeling results and market adoption requirements. • Targeted climate region / Building Profile / Grid Integration –modeling results will be leveraged to determine in which climate regions / buildings / and grids the proposed technology will have the most desirable impacts. • Performance Indices - the following are example of performance metrics that can increase market adoption in targeted applications. o System efficiency o TES round trip efficiency and charging/discharging duration o Instantaneous and integrated capacities o Connectivity and demand response capabilities will be evaluated based on economic benefits offered by utilities. • Information dissemination – this task will explore partnerships with utilities to initiate new assessment projects to qualify the technology for inclusion in the incentive programs. Additionally, this task will spread the awareness of the project through various venues including conferences and journal publications. As part of Task 6, NREL and NETenergy held meetings with various electric utilities about the benefits of the technology for managing peak load. We also presented on this technology at venues attended by several HVAC manufacturers, including the Herrick Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Conference, the ASME Summer Heat Transfer Conference, as well as the Building Technologies Office Peer Review. Task 7: Final Evaluation Task Summary: Following Task 6, each party will perform its own final evaluation of the HVAC + thermal storage system and the parties will meet in good faith to discuss whether to continue working on the technology in future phases and in what capacity This task was originally proposed for this CRADA project, but this Gen-2 prototype was not delivered to NREL for evaluation. Task 8 and 9: Modeling and design of high-power PCM heat exchanger, and bench-scale experimental validation For this task, we designed two thermal storage prototypes with extremely fast discharge rates (discharge in ~5 minutes). The first prototype used glycol as the working fluid, with a target discharge power of 1 kW and a total energy of 0.1 kWh.
